newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Protests reach Bulgarian left's nuclear stronghold.
newsitem.headline: Protests reach Bulgarian left's nuclear stronghold.

text.p: Bulgaria's tide of unrest washed into the pro-government stronghold of Kozloduy on Thursday, but won only little support from well-paid nuclear workers capable of bringing the national economy to a halt.
Only around 20 staff of the huge Kozloduy plant, which produces more than 40 percent of the country's electricity, attended a 1,000-strong rally against the ruling Socialists.

Most protesters came from surrounding countryside. They were faced by residents of a Danube town with a 70-year pro-communist tradition who were pampered as elite workers in an industrial showcase of the former communist regime.
Almost every Kozloduy family has a member working at the nuclear plant, and onlookers watched the march against the ex-communist Socialists stony-faced from pavements and windows.
In contrast to the scene at other demonstrations across Bulgaria over the last 11 days, most declined invitations to join the rally and neither waved hands in support nor smiled.
"We don't think things will get better that way," said one couple of the rally. "This should be politicians' concern."
The Kozloduy workers appear very unlikely to test a law which specifically bans them from striking. But among the few nuclear workers to turn out at Thursday's rally was engineer Emil Sherbanov, 32.
"We walked out onto the streets to protest against misery, no matter that we are well paid," he said.

"We're well off compared to most Bulgarian people but our standard of living is constantly falling compared to our colleagues at Western nuclear power plants. I have a child and I want hope for children."

Miroslav Marinov, 33, another engineer, said he supported opposition demands -- the main one being for elections soon which the Socialists would almost certainly lose. An opinion poll gave them just eight percent support on Thursday.
"The only way for things to improve is to change the current majority in parliament," Marinov said.
In contrast to the state-employed nuclear workers was Lyuben Iliev, a private farmer from the village of Butan, who bemoaned government failure to reform the state-run economy.

"The communists do not let private property develop because it will allow us to become independent," he said, adding he could cultivate only half his land because of lack of equipment and cash to buy seed.
Fellow-villager Suleiman Bairamov agreed. "I am unemployed because the communists provided no jobs for us," he said. "The money is with them. Have you met any rich men among ordinary working people?"
Living standards for most Bulgarians have plunged under inflation of more than 300 percent a year and the collapse of the lev currency. Typical salaries are worth $10-20 a month.
The rally was organised by the opposition Podkrepa trade union, which appealed to the nuclear plant's staff to say "no to impoverishment, humiliation, destruction, misery and fear".
Bulgaria switched off the Soviet-made reactor number one at the 3,760-megawatt Kozloduy plant on May 15 for tests after the international community expressed concern over its safety.
The 440-megawatt reactor is planned to be restarted by the end of this week after tests showing it to be safe, carried out by German firm Siemens AG and Bulgarian experts.
